description: Seven generations of Buendía in Macondo. García Márquez mixes wonders and tragedy to tell Latin American history.

hero.hook: A shower of yellow flowers or a woman who ascends to heaven: the marvelous told as an ordinary event.

blocks.text: Published in **1967**,  is the worldwide birth certificate of . This style presents magical events with the same naturalness as real events, without surprises or explanations. **Gabriel García Márquez**, born in **1927** and died in **2014**, retraces seven generations of the Buendía family in **Macondo**, a fictional village inspired by his hometown. [[A hundred years of solitude]] [[Magical realism]]

Political violence, economic imperialism and ancestral myths intertwine. By breaking the linearity of time, the author makes wonder and tragedy coexist with disconcerting evidence. A shower of yellow flowers or an ascension to heaven are recounted as ordinary events.

**Gabriel García Márquez**, known as “Gabo”, draws from **Aracataca**, his Colombian hometown. His grandfather tells him about the civil wars; her grandmother recounts ghosts and omens with imperturbable seriousness. This way of telling the marvelous without commenting on it becomes the key to his style.

blocks.caption: Gabriel García Márquez, the Nobel Prize winner who made Latin America heard by the whole world.

blocks.text: In **1965**, García Márquez had his enlightenment while driving to Acapulco. He turned around and isolated himself for 18 months to write, while his wife pawned their property.

The first print run of **8,000 copies** sold out in a few days in Buenos Aires. The author will receive the **Nobel Prize for Literature** in **1982**, consecrating a novel that has become emblematic of an entire continental literature.

sections.title: The Genesis of a Style: Aracataca and Enlightenment

blocks.text: **José Arcadio Buendía** founded Macondo in the Colombian jungle. The village goes through the ages: innocence, technology brought by the gypsies, then political corruption. **Colonel Aureliano Buendía** leads thirty-two armed uprisings and loses them all. He embodies the tragic repetition of Latin American history.

blocks.caption: Macondo: a tropical village where the history of Latin America is condensed.

blocks.text: The arrival of  transposes the banana plantation massacre of **1928** to Colombia. Thousands of striking workers are shot, then a flood erases the memory of the event. García Márquez shows how economic imperialism and collective forgetting destroy people. [[The United Fruit Company and the "banana republics"]]

sections.title: Macondo: between mythical foundation and brutal reality

blocks.text: When **Remedies the Beautiful** ascends to heaven by folding sheets, the narrator shows no surprise. The magical is an organic extension of reality, not a decorative fantasy. This is the golden rule of : the marvelous is part of everyday life. [[Magical realism]]

The weather in Macondo is **circular**: the Buendías repeat the errors of their ancestors, confuse first names, fall back into the same passions. The manuscript of **Melquíades**, written in , the coded language of prophecies, tells the family's history a hundred years in advance. At the final reading, a cyclone destroys Macondo: the cycle closes. [[Sanskrit]]

sections.title: The mechanics of the unusual and the circularity of time

blocks.text: The novel paved the way for the Latin American “**Boom**”. This literary movement marks the years **1960**-**1970**. Authors like  are among them. The novel proved that the story could be the site of a modern mythology as powerful as Antiquity. [[Mario Vargas Llosa]]

García Márquez shows the erosion of idealism through war and collective forgetting. Without memory or solidarity, civilizations are ephemeral, condemned to repeat tragedy. Macondo is not just a village: it is a condensed Latin American memory, where the marvelous and the political touch.
García Márquez's  uses the marvelous to tell the historical truth and the tragic solitude of Latin America. [[Magical realism]]
